extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for preparing and construing patent specifications, drawings, disclaimers, and claims (how they must be signed, what they must disclose, how drawings and text interact, and how courts interpret claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire specification and drawings examined together
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire specification and drawings are to be examined together, and an error in one place to be corrected by the aid of the residue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The drawings need not be mentioned in the specification, but it is sufficient if the patentee puts them and written references on file with the specification. Courts read the written description and drawings together to determine sufficiency and scope (cases cited: Hogg v. Emerson, Kittle v. Merriam, Emmerson v. Hogg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-filed drawing admissible in evidence but not part of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing filed some time after the recording anew of a patent, under section one, act March, 1837, is admissible in evidence, but is not to be deemed and taken as part of the specification, nor to be used for correcting any material defect therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such late drawings may be shown to a court but cannot be used to cure material defects in the original specification (cited: Winans v. Schenectady & Troy R.R.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings need not be to scale
rubrics_metrics.description: It was formerly held ... that the drawings annexed to specifications ought to be drawn on a scale ... But this rule has been modified; and it seems now to be considered that if a mechanic can make the subject of the patent from the drawing in perspective, it is not necessary that there should be a scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the written description and drawing explain each other, scale is immaterial so long as both together enable the public to know and practise the invention. However, if the subject could not be made without many experiments unless the drawing is on a scale, then the combined specification (written + drawing) would be defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal attestation/signature requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires a formal attestation of the specification and drawings. They must be signed by the inventor and by two witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier statutes required the description and drawings to be signed by the inventor and attested by two witnesses. It has been suggested that signing the specification referring to the drawings effectively attests the drawings, but whether both must be separately signed was not definitively decided in earlier cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of 1870 signature and drawings attachment rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of 1870 provides that the 'specification and claim shall be signed by the inventor, and attested by two witnesses'; and a copy of the drawings 'shall be attached to the patent, as part of the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the 1870 statute the specification and claim must be signed/attested and drawings are to be attached to the patent as part of the specification — affecting formal sufficiency and the record on the patent itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment by adding improvements (historical rule and repeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision was made by the thirteenth section of the act of 1836 for the amendment of the specification by the addition of new improvements made after the patent has issued. ... This provision was repealed by the act of 1861 ... and in all cases where additional improvements would now be admissible, independent patents must be applied for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements entered before the repealing clause remain valid under the act of 1836; after repeal, new improvements generally require separate patent filings (see chapter on Proceedings at Patent Office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer to correct overbroad specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever any patentee shall have, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, made his specification of claim too broad, claiming more than that of which he was the original or first inventor ... any such patentee ... may make disclaimer of such parts of the thing patented as the disclaimant shall not claim to hold by virtue of the patent or assignment, ... which disclaimer shall be in writing, attested by one or more witnesses, and recorded in the Patent Office, on payment ... of the sum of ten dollars. And such disclaimer shall thereafter be taken and considered as part of the original specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer allows a patentee to limit an overbroad claim; it must be written, witnessed, recorded, and (historically) a fee paid. It becomes part of the original specification to the extent stated, but cannot affect pending actions except as to unreasonable neglect or delay in filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of 1870 disclaimer provision (patent valid for bona fide part)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention, a patentee has claimed more than that of which he was the original or first inventor or discoverer, his patent shall be valid for all that part which is truly and justly his own, provided the same is a material or substantial part of the thing patented; and any such patentee ... may, on payment of the duty required by law, make disclaimer ... and it shall thereafter be considered as part of the original specification ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute preserves validity for the material/substantial part actually invented and permits recorded disclaimers to limit the patent. A disclaimer does not affect actions pending at filing time except regarding unreasonable neglect or delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and effect distinction between disclaimers (§7 vs §9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclaimer mentioned in the seventh section has been held to apply solely to suits pending when the disclaimer was filed in the Patent Office; and that mentioned in the ninth section, to suits brought after the disclaimer is so filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts interpret different statutory disclaimer provisions to harmonize their legal effect: one governs suits already pending, the other suits subsequently brought (see Wyeth v. Stone and Story J.'s exposition). Timing of filing a disclaimer affects remedies and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on disclaimers: cannot be used to convert impracticable generality into valid specific claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer that attempts to turn a specification for an impracticable generality into a claim for a specific process which cannot be discovered from the specification without conducting the same experiments as led to the discovery is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the desired specific process is not disclosed in the original specification and would require the same experimental work to discover, a later disclaimer cannot validly create that specific claim (illustrated by Ralston v. Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional specification cannot explain or enlarge complete specification
rubrics_metrics.description: By the statute ... an inventor is allowed to make a provisional specification, pending the proceedings for obtaining letters-patent. In Mackelcan v. Rennie, it was held that such provisional specification is not to be admitted in explanation or enlargement of the complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A provisional specification cannot be invoked to cure deficiencies or expand the meaning of the later complete specification when determining scope or sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must set forth materials, proportions, and processes (sufficiency of disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee has set forth fully the materials, their various proportions, and the processes necessary to the production of this composition of matter, he has done all that the law requires ... It should show what the patentee claims to have discovered or invented, wherein it differs from what was heretofore known, and by what combinations or processes the new material may be compounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For compositions or new products, disclose ingredients, proportions, and necessary processes. The description should show nature and design, separate new from old where feasible, and enable production without undue experimentation. Courts will not penalize imperfect language so long as the discovery and process are set forth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show what is old vs what is new (separation of new from old)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essentially proper, in patents for complicated machines, that the specification should clearly set forth what the patentee admits to be old and what he claims to be of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful separation of new from old and limitation of claims to particular parts or combinations is recommended, though not always required as a substantial part of the specification; clarifies boundaries of monopoly and aids construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be construed as machine, process, product, or result depending on description
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee's claim must be construed according to its words, and in view of the specification and the nature of the thing described; claims for a machine must be read as one for a machine, and not for a process or result, and vice versa (illustrated in Kay v. Marshall and other cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine both the language of the claim and the specification context to determine whether the claim is for a machine, a process, a composition, or merely a result. Mislabeling or ambiguous wording will be interpreted against overly broad readings; examples include Kay (machine vs result), McCormick, and Goodyear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-oriented claim may be construed as claim to means/mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim in words for the result was in reality for the means or mechanism by which that result was to be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim is worded as a claim to a result, if the specification describes particular means or mechanisms, courts will construe the claim as limited to those means or their equivalents (example: Howe's sewing-machine claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims can be valid despite prior use of components
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim for the manner of arranging and connecting parts in combination may be a valid claim for the device itself; the novelty of the invention is not necessarily impeached by evidence showing that parts of the invention had been in use previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel arrangement/combination of known parts can be patentable; claim construction looks to the arrangement as claimed (example: Winans' car construction and McCormick's arrangement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue cannot broaden to an abstract principle; overly elastic claims invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: An attempt to convert an improved machine into an abstraction, a principle, or mode of operation by use of general and abstract terms, making the specification so elastic that it might be construed to claim all means for the same purpose, is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissues or amended claims that broaden the patent to cover abstract principles beyond the inventor's disclosed contribution are subject to invalidation (illustrated by Burr v. Duryee). Care must be taken not to draft claims unbounded by the disclosed mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate claims are to be read independently unless text indicates otherwise
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims (e.g., No. 2 and No. 3 in McCormick's patent) were not to be read in connection with each other, but separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim stands on its own for construction: do not assume dependent linkage among distinct claims unless the specification explicitly makes them dependent.
